title: Justice for all
hookLine: the good of all includes standing for the wronged

lines: SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.
cards: The Sikh ardas, the standing prayer at the end of a service, closes on a wish for the whole world. Tere bhane sarbat da bhala: in your will, the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs.
Not the good of the people in the room. Everyone. It's a lovely wish to say aloud, and a hard one to mean.
Because once the good of all is the goal, someone being trampled is no longer somebody else's business. Guru Nanak once watched a city being trampled, and what he said about it is where today begins.

teach.h: THE BABARVANI: DID YOU FEEL NO PAIN?
teach.b: First, the cry. When Babur's armies swept in, Guru Nanak, tradition says, saw the slaughter with his own eyes. His hymns about it are called the Babarvani.

In one, in Raag Asa, he speaks straight to God. In paraphrase: such suffering, such crying out, and did You feel no pain? He describes women whose hair was once braided for weddings, now dragged and shamed.
A hymn can be a protest. Second, naming it plainly.

teach.h: TILANG: SAY THE WRONG BY ITS NAME.
teach.b: In Raag Tilang he calls the invading host a wedding party of sin, and says he will speak the word of truth, because the time for truth has come. No flattery of the powerful.
Justice starts with refusing to call a wrong anything else. Third, the good of all.

teach.h: SARBAT DA BHALA INCLUDES THE WRONGED.
teach.b: If sarbat da bhala is real, it includes the people being wronged, and it lays a claim on whoever sees it. Sikh memory keeps stories, from the Gurus to the Khalsa, of standing up for people who weren't their own.
Fourth, the small stakes. Few of us will ever face an army. But someone is talked over in a meeting.
Someone gets the cruel nickname. Someone's rent goes unfixed because they won't complain.

teach.h: A WORD, A WITNESS, A SEAT BESIDE.
teach.b: Standing for them might mean a word, a witness, a phone call, a seat beside them.
Guru Nanak had no army to send. He had a hymn, and he sang it.

how: Sikhs end the ardas with sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and remember Guru Nanak's Babarvani hymns as a protest against the suffering of ordinary people.

o: the good of all, which includes standing up for the wronged
a court where Sikhs settle disputes among themselves
a promise that the guilty will be punished in time

games.q: justice for all: tap the pairs.
p: Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's slaughter

s: the ardas closes with a wish for Sikhs only
it closes with sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
Guru Nanak spoke straight to God about the suffering he saw
in Raag Asa: such suffering, and did You feel no pain?
the Babarvani praises the conquering army
it names the slaughter plainly and speaks for the people trampled.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and an army has just trampled the city around you. what do you do with your hymns?
o: keep them on quieter, safer themes.
praise the new ruler to protect your people.
cry out about the suffering and name the wrong.
games.why: the Babarvani asks God, did You feel no pain? and calls the invasion a wedding party of sin.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is being treated unfairly, near you or far away, and don't rush past their face. Breathe in and see what they're carrying; breathe out and ask what one true thing you could say or do for them.
Let one small answer become clear.

wordCard.voice: Justice for all. Sarbat da bhala, the good of all, includes standing for the wronged, as Guru Nanak did when he cried out against Babur's slaughter. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sarbat da bhala, the good of all, the closing wish of the ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: stand for others. One true sentence on someone's behalf is within anyone's reach. Back tomorrow, same hill.
